risks.title: When they slip away
risks.body: In a CPSC study of young children who drowned in pools in Arizona, California and Florida, 46% were last seen in the house, 69% weren’t expected to be at or in the pool, and 77% had been missing for 5 minutes or less.

risks.title: When the house is full
risks.body: Parties, holidays and cookouts are when doors get propped open, alarms get switched off, and a toddler can slip away without anyone noticing. Name a Water Watcher and keep every layer on.

risks.title: At someone else’s home
risks.body: Grandparents’, neighbors’ and friends’ pools count too. More than 70% of children who die in a pool or spa drown at a home, including the homes of family, friends and neighbors.

risks.title: In the bathtub
risks.body: Babies under 1 most often drown in bathtubs. Young children can drown in just an inch or two of water, so stay within arm’s reach at bath time and empty buckets and kiddie pools.

risks.title: In summer, and all year
risks.body: Pool and spa drownings peak in June, July and August. But bathtubs, buckets, hot tubs and ponds don’t take the winter off. Keep every layer in place in every season.

risks.title: Children with autism
risks.body: Among people with autism, deaths are nearly 40 times as likely to be caused by drowning as deaths in the general population. Children on the autism spectrum may be drawn to water and not always recognize the danger. Door alarms, adapted swim lessons and a wandering plan help.

facts.label: Drowning is the leading cause of death for children ages 1–4.
facts.detail: It happens most often in home pools, and layers of protection help prevent it.

facts.label: Children under 15 who drown in a pool or spa each year, on average (2021–2023).
facts.detail: Nearly 80% of them were younger than 5.

facts.label: Toddlers are at the highest risk of drowning.
facts.detail: They can slip away without anyone noticing, even under the best of circumstances.

facts.label: Lives lost to unintentional drowning each year in the U.S. (2020–2022).
facts.detail: That’s about 500 more each year than in 2019.

facts.label: Drowning is the second leading cause of unintentional-injury death for children ages 5–14, after car crashes.
Black children ages 10–14 drown in swimming pools at 7.6 times the rate of White children (1999–2019).

groups.title: Nonfatal drowning
groups.intro: Many children survive a drowning. Some recover completely. Others, like Adam, live with injuries that last a lifetime, such as brain injury or permanent disability.

groups.title: What protects children
groups.intro: The good news: drowning is preventable, and the layers of protection work best together.

facts.label: Lower odds of drowning with a fence that isolates the pool on all four sides, compared with three-sided fencing.
facts.detail: When the house is one side of the fence, a toddler can walk straight out the back door to the water.

facts.label: Toddlers and weak swimmers need an adult within arm’s reach, “touch supervision,” whenever they’re in or near water.
facts.detail: Name a Water Watcher so there’s never a question of who’s watching.

facts.label: Swim lessons after a child’s first birthday are linked to a lower drowning risk for young children.
facts.detail: The benefit is real but hard to size precisely, and lessons never replace supervision or barriers.

facts.label: Fast CPR with rescue breaths matters after a drowning. Our mom started CPR on Adam right away.
facts.detail: In an emergency, call 911. Take an infant and child CPR class, and renew it every two years.
